Distributed Collaboration between Industry and University Partners in Higher Education by Erik Bohemia* Neil Smith** Kerry Harman*** Trevor Duncan**** Chris Turnock***** and Sung-Gul Hwang****** * School of Design, Northumbria University, Newcastle upon Tyne, NE1 8ST, United Kingdom, erik.bohemia@northumbria.ac.uk City, Country (Blank if Blind Review), e-mail address (Blank if Blind Review) ** School of Design, Northumbria University, Newcastle upon Tyne, NE1 8ST, United Kingdom, neil.smith@northumbria.ac.uk *** Centre for Excellence in Teaching & Learning in Assessment for Learning, Northumbria University, Newcastle upon Tyne, NE1 8ST, United Kingdom, kerry.harman@northumbria.ac.uk **** School of Design, Northumbria University, Newcastle upon Tyne, NE1 8ST, United Kingdom, ***** LTech, Northumbria University Newcastle upon Tyne, NE1 8ST, United Kingdom, chris.turnock@northumbria.ac.uk ****** Consumer Experience Design Mobile Devices, Motorola Korea Hibrand, Yangjaedong 215, Seochogu, Seoul, Korea, sung-gul.hwang@motorola.com Abstract: The School of Design has been innovating over the last three years with a curriculum approach known as ‘the Global Studio’. This initiative represents a collaborative platform for teaching and learning that integrates research across institutions involving Northumbria University and international universities and industry partners from the UK, USA, Netherlands, and Korea. The objectives of the Global Studio are explicitly connected to the evolving needs of the industry in terms of the organization of product and service development. These shifts underscore the necessity of preparing design students with competencies suited for global networks, particularly in intercultural communication and collaborative skills. This paper will highlight the 2008 iteration of the Global Studio, which saw participation from Northumbria University (UK), Hongik University (Korea), Auburn University (USA), Intel (USA), Motorola design studios in the UK and Korea, and Great Southern Wood (USA). The documented projects offer insights into both the challenges and advantages of undertaking industry-based international collaborations in distributed environments. Key words: Global Studio; Industry-Based Projects; International Collaboration.
For the last three years, Northumbria University's School of Design has been trying out a fresh approach to curriculum design and delivery called 'the Global Studio'. This innovative model is a collaboration for teaching and learning based on research between Northumbria University and various international universities and industry partners. The participating institutions and companies include TU Delft, Napier University, Hongik University, Ohio State University, Auburn University, and RMIT University, along with Intel Corp., Motorola, Great Southern Wood, and Inverness Medical Innovation, all located in the UK, USA, Netherlands, Australia, and Korea. The Global Studio’s objectives are closely tied to both current and future industry needs, particularly changes in how products and services are developed. These shifts emphasize the necessity of preparing design students to work in globally networked organizations, especially by developing skills in intercultural communication and collaboration. This paper focuses on the Global Studio conducted in 2008. It will briefly introduce the joint projects undertaken by Northumbria University with its industry partners in the USA and Korea. We will then discuss the interaction and communication within the project teams. Our analysis will use evaluation data collected from UK-based students during the projects and upon their completion. Observations from two of the authors, who were involved in the delivery of the Global Studio, will also contribute to the data set.
The inaugural Global Studio was envisioned as a yearly course jointly conducted by universities from various countries. A primary goal of the Global Studio was to create a learning environment where students could hone skills in intercultural communication and collaboration in a financially sustainable manner, allowing participation from the entire student cohort. Another objective was to establish a system permitting each partner university to independently manage teaching and assessment, thus addressing some challenges tied to cross-institutional collaborations [1]. In the initial course, student roles and activities were organized throughout the project to foster cross-institutional interaction. This was mainly accomplished by having students take on the dual roles of client and designer. An in-depth explanation of how the client and designer roles were set up is available elsewhere [1]. The following year, a different program within the School of Design embraced the Global Studio, aiming not only for collaboration with university partners but also with industry partners located in various regions. Integrating industry partners introduced additional challenges compared to the earlier Global Studio. For instance, the presence of industry partners increased the complexity of communication and interaction among students, lecturers, and the industry partners (see Figure 1 and Figure 2). Figure 1 portrays the interactions between student teams and lecturers in the Global Studio conducted in 20072 1 Data collected reflects the views primarily of Northumbria University students, as only UK-based students completed the project exit surveys unless specified otherwise. 2 Note: Multiple work teams were positioned at each partner university 236 Figure 2 highlights the heightened complexity of interactions between student teams, industry partners, and lecturers in the Global Studio conducted in 20082. The addition of three industry partners also influenced the structure of projects and the roles and activities of students. For instance, in the 2008 Global Studio, it was the industry partners who assumed the role of clients. Consequently, students from the participating universities no longer acted as 'clients' and 'designers' for one another, as they had in the previous Global Studio, which markedly altered their interaction and communication with each other.
In this section, we'll provide a brief overview of the industry-based projects undertaken during the 2008 Global Studio. Three collaborative projects were introduced: ‘Constructing Constructs’, ‘Thinking Outside the Box’, and ‘On the Move’. These projects were completed with various industry and university partners (see Table 1). The ‘Constructing Constructs’ project involved collaboration between Northumbria University and Hong-ik University in Korea, alongside Motorola’s design studios in the UK and Korea. Motorola’s Korean Design office also contributed a staff member who taught a class for 10 third-year industrial design students at the Korean university. This project delved into two sub-themes: ‘Constructing Luxury’ and ‘Constructing Technology’ [3]. The second project, ‘Thinking Outside the Box’, was a partnership between universities in the UK and USA, working with Great Southern Wood, a USA-based timber company. Final-year industrial design students at Auburn University participated, and the project was coordinated by a lecturer there. The ‘On the Move’ project was commissioned by the multinational semiconductor company, Intel, and conducted between Northumbria University and the company's USA office. It covered three sub-themes: ‘Design for Experience’, ‘Imagining a Notebook’, and ‘Futures of Mobile Computing’. Thirty-four third-year Industrial Design students from Northumbria University participated in all the projects, choosing which project to join. Ten students selected the ‘On the Move’ project, 12 chose ‘Thinking Outside the Box’, and 12 worked on ‘Constructing Constructs’. Additionally, Master of Design students observed some of these projects as part of their Design Management studies. Although not directly involved in designing, their presence was appreciated by the undergraduates, who found them ‘a wealth of knowledge’. Each project group was split into smaller teams. There were six teams per university for ‘Thinking Outside the Box’, and three linked teams for ‘Constructing Constructs’. Table 1 outlines the work teams: Partners Industry-Based Projects Constructing Constructs Northumbria University (UK) 3 groups, each with 4 members Hong-ik University (Korea) 3 groups, each with 3 members Motorola, a multinational mobile phone maker (UK and Korea) Thinking Outside the Box Northumbria University (UK) 6 groups, each with 2 members Auburn University (USA) 6 groups, each with 2 members Great Southern Wood, a national USA timber company On the Move Northumbria University (UK) 10 to 7 students Intel, a multinational semiconductor company (USA) In the ‘On the Move’ project, students worked on individual concepts but were encouraged to pair up at different stages, like idea generation. They presented as a group to the industry partner rather than individually.
The ‘On the Move’ project began with a visit from an industry representative to Northumbria University, who introduced the project team to three broad sub-themes: ‘Design for Experience,’ ‘Imagining a Notebook,’ and ‘Futures of Mobile Computing.’ These sub-themes each targeted different time frames for design solutions. ‘Design for Experience’ focused on present-day solutions, ‘Imagining a Notebook’ projected four years into the future, and ‘Futures of Mobile Computing’ looked beyond the four-year horizon. Students were tasked with interpreting the requirements and drafting a brief to discuss with industry representatives. The only restriction was that any proposed device’s screen could not be smaller than specified by the company. Throughout the project, the ‘On the Move’ industry partners made regular visits to Northumbria University for face-to-face meetings and project reviews. The Motorola representative set sub-themes that fell under two broader themes: ‘New Luxury’ (Constructing Luxury) and ‘New Digital Lifestyle’ (Constructing Technology). A teleconference that connected UK and Korean universities with industry partner representatives was utilized for a briefing session, which included a presentation. The industry representative’s sole request was the exclusion of phones, initially causing uncertainty among the team who expected the project to align with the company’s product line, such as mobile phones. Once again, student groups were prompted to create a design brief based on one of the two sub-themes. For the ‘Thinking Outside the Box’ project, a lecturer from Auburn University, who organized the industry project, conducted a briefing session. Students at Northumbria University were paired with counterparts from Auburn University, and the UK students were asked to develop a design brief that complemented the work of their US counterparts.
After the briefing sessions, students were instructed to post an introduction and a photo of themselves on the project wiki pages. Next, the work teams needed to establish a shared space for their collaboration, which involved creating (i) a wiki page, (ii) a team name, (iii) a logo, and subsequently (iv) uploading design briefs onto their specific project wiki pages. This was followed by a virtual meeting with other partners to discuss the design briefs. Once these were mutually agreed upon, the teams conducted research to explore potential approaches for addressing the design briefs. Research results were then reviewed to guide the development of concepts, which were further analyzed to direct subsequent revisions and iterations of the design proposals. This process culminated in the presentation of a final design proposal to industry partner representatives. Presentation outputs varied among different project workgroups and within individual workgroups. For instance, the 'On the Move' project featured a series of two-minute animations highlighting the key benefits of each design concept, compiled into a standalone DVD presentation. 'Constructing Constructs' incorporated a mix of storyboards and multimedia animation presentations. The 'Thinking Outside the Box' project used storyboards and scale models to illustrate the working principles of various design proposals. The three projects employed a range of communication tools to facilitate both asynchronous and synchronous communication, structured according to the available communication equipment at each participating partner organization and the IT policies of the UK-based university. Students were able to collaborate in both collocated and distributed settings, engaging with various communication technologies for synchronous and asynchronous interactions. For instance, they worked in collocated environments and communicated synchronously when collaborating with teammates from the same institution (top left quadrant in Figure 3). Figure 3 Dimensions of collaboration [based on 4] Work team members from the same institutions also used asynchronous tools like email and wiki pages (top right quadrant in Figure 3). Additionally, they operated in distributed settings and communicated synchronously through tele/videoconferencing with partners in different geographic locations (bottom left quadrant in Figure 3). Asynchronous tools, such as email and wiki pages, were also utilized to communicate with partners in other locations (bottom right quadrant in Figure 3).
To facilitate asynchronous communication, each project was assigned secured, dedicated wiki pages utilizing MediaWiki software. These pages were hosted by Northumbria University and were chosen as a communication tool for several reasons: 

- A web-based service was available, allowing users unrestricted access to create, edit, and link pages, as per the 2009 Committee of Inquiry into the Changing Learner Experience's report on Higher Education in a Web 2.0 World.
- External collaborators could access these project-specific wiki pages, unlike the university's existing online learning system (i.e., Blackboard), which was limited to enrolled students and university staff.
- Users with individual log-ins enjoyed unrestricted access to create, edit, and link pages, facilitating flexibility in structuring their group or individual project wiki pages.
- Basic text editing on wikis doesn't require HTML coding knowledge, and standard files could be uploaded to the wikis without needing special external software like a web editor or FTP client.

The intention was for design teams to upload their work, such as design briefs, research including mind maps, mood boards, videos, sketches, and other visual representations of design concepts, storyboards, and multimedia files such as animations and movies, onto their project-specific wiki pages. These pages were accessible to participants at each location during scheduled synchronous project meetings, allowing them to present and review the project alongside the materials on the wiki pages.
Although all students completed the initial exercise, many had trouble using the wiki pages. Some opted out entirely, especially those from Auburn University, who preferred Facebook for asynchronous communication with their UK counterparts instead of the project wiki pages. Consequently, UK students involved in the 'Thinking Outside the Box' also switched to Facebook. One UK student mentioned enjoying the video/teleconferencing experience, gaining new skills and confidence in presenting ideas through various mediums. However, the student they collaborated with failed to use the wiki pages despite repeated requests, resulting in minimal contributions due to concerns about wastage. Students from the USA reported issues with frequently overwriting wiki pages, files, and images, as highlighted by one student's comment: "The wiki page was a pain in the ass. Loading images was a huge headache. As our class wasn’t familiar with the system, several students placed pages incorrectly, overwriting others' work." This problem arose from the 'flat' structure of wiki pages, unlike HTML-based pages that use folders. Consequently, each new wiki page and uploaded files or images required unique names to prevent overwriting existing content. For instance, if one student uploaded a photo named 'my photo.jpg,' another uploading the same name would overwrite it. Although a warning appeared about identical names, students often continued, overwriting someone else’s photo, an action only apparent if they checked the affected person's wiki pages. Students universally criticized the wikis for their poor editing interface, inadequate file uploading facilities, and slow speeds. To address these limitations, teams working on the 'Constructing Constructs' project uploaded large multimedia files to free file sharing sites, then linked these files on the project wiki pages. This workaround introduced new issues, such as the removal of project files from a secure web environment, raising confidentiality concerns, and link expiration after a few days. Furthermore, many free file-sharing sites advertised adult content or software that could potentially infect a visitor’s computer. Despite wiki-related challenges, students appreciated having a web space to share project progress, as one remarked: "Wiki pages can be tricky to grasp, but it's good to have a place to share ideas and work." They valued having their work (e.g., multimedia files) accessible online to student teams and industry partners for explaining ideas over phone or videoconference. Observing others’ work was beneficial, as students noted: "It was good to see how everyone tackles the project uniquely," and "We can compare each other's learning methods." This transparency also added an element of competition, as one student expressed: "It pushes you to work to your potential, seeing real competition. Engaging with others enhances your work."
During the 2008 Global Studio, the university in the UK enforced IT policies that restricted the use of all messaging and Voice over Internet Protocol (VoIP) applications. This limitation meant that software supporting real-time communication, like AOL Messenger, MSN Messenger, Yahoo! Messenger, NetMeeting, ooVoo, and Skype, was inaccessible to participants from the UK university when using the university’s network. As a result, students and faculty couldn’t engage in live discussions with external partners using internet-based messaging and VoIP tools. Consequently, synchronous interactions relied on traditional phones or video conferencing equipment. Teleconferencing became the primary method for real-time communication on projects such as ‘Constructing Constructs’ and ‘On the Move,’ with industry partners organizing and funding these meetings. These sessions typically lasted two hours or more, with each session costing around £100. For example, a Motorola representative based in the UK facilitated a three-way teleconference bridge to connect the universities in the UK and Korea with the industry partner. Regular video conferences occurred between the UK and USA universities as they both had standard video conferencing equipment. As only university phones and video conferencing gear were available for use, scheduling these meetings required advance planning by lecturers and industry partners. This restriction meant that while the UK students were primarily working from the university, spontaneous conversations with external partners were impossible without incurring significant personal phone costs. Student teams, mainly using teleconferencing and wiki pages for the 'Constructing Constructs' and 'On the Move’ projects, expressed a preference for video conferencing, believing it would allow for clearer idea explanation and concept demonstration. They also noted challenges with speakerphone audio quality. Meanwhile, the ‘Thinking Outside the Box’ teams, who mainly used video conferencing for meetings and chose not to use the project wiki pages, found it difficult to present concepts effectively through video conferences. Teams from the ‘On the Move’ project met face-to-face with industry representatives several times (see Table 3), yet only one student highlighted the importance of these in-person meetings. The varied availability and usage of communication tools led to differences in the technologies used by project teams during their work (see Table 2 below).  

**Table 2: Communication Technologies**

| Email                    | Yes                     | Yes                      | Yes         |

All of the industry-based projects got underway in February. However, the 'On the Move' project wrapped up 2 ½ months after the other two initiatives. Table 3 provides a summary of the meeting frequency for each project's communication, as well as the duration of the projects. It also details the kinds of technology used for communication and whether industry partners were involved. For instance, industry partners participated in every communication session for both the 'Constructing the Construct' and 'On the Move' projects. In contrast, the industry partner for 'Thinking Outside the Box' only joined the UK-based workgroups in the second half of the project. Notably, this project's workgroups exclusively used videoconferencing for meetings. The 'On the Move' project teams, over a 20-week period, held nine meetings with industry partners. Four were in-person meetings, with USA-based industry staff traveling to meet the UK project team. The 'Constructing the Construct' work teams had seven meetings with university and industry partners during the 10-week span of their project. During the same period, the 'Thinking Outside the Box' teams conducted an equal number of meetings, mostly through videoconferencing. However, only two of these meetings involved the industry partner and the UK-based teams. 

Table 3: Frequency and Type of Communication Between Distributed Partners From February to March:

Key: Underline signifies communication included industry partners. T - Teleconferencing | FtF - Face-to-Face | V - Videoconferencing

Generally, students involved in the 'Thinking Outside the Box' project rated their experiences less satisfying compared to those in the other two project groups. They also rated lower on the effectiveness of project phases like writing a design brief, communicating design concepts, reviewing design progress, and presenting the final design proposal. Conversely, over 80% of the students in the other two projects rated these phases as working 'very well' or 'well.' Yet, even those working on the 'Thinking Outside the Box' project acknowledged that their engagement in the Global Studio enhanced their skills in remote communication. They also encountered challenges related to distributed communication, as reflected in the following comments:

- It has made me realize the difficulty of cross-country communication.
- First time using Wiki pages and videoconferencing, now I know why it's so challenging!

These sentiments were echoed by students in the other groups. Shared themes among all project workgroups included increased confidence in public speaking and presenting ideas, as well as using various communication technologies. For example, one student from the 'On the Move' project said their:

- confidence in discussing ideas with people from different countries has grown.

Another stated:

- I have gained more confidence in my communication skills due to the weekly meetings.

Overall, students felt the course improved their remote communication skills, and most agreed that the Global Studio helped them understand better the challenges of working with distributed design teams and clients. Korean students noted that the Global Studio offered them a chance to practice and improve their English skills. Many students viewed their learning experiences positively, recognizing the benefits gained from participating in the Global Studio. For instance:

- Through this project, I learned experientially, gaining free-thinking, confidence, and the ability to face challenges.
- Learned how communication over the internet can easily go wrong.
- Communicating online without body language was challenging for me.
- I realized how difficult long-distance communication can be.
- I developed skills across different communication media.
- Talking to a real client and working with Korean students improved my team skills.
- Describing everything in detail both online and in-person improved my communication skills.
- I became aware of how much I rely on speech and explanation.
Overall, students expressed that they enjoyed their learning experience in the Global Studio. They all felt an improvement in their communication skills thanks to working with international university and industry partners. However, they also noted challenges in using communication technologies, particularly the wiki pages. A study entitled ‘The Great Expectations of ICT’ [6], which examined first-year students' experiences with ICT in the UK Higher Education sector, found that students were both unfamiliar and uncomfortable with wiki pages. The report argues that this technology currently pushes students 'beyond their comfort zones' [7]. Findings from the Global Studio indicate that students need more support through training and accessible tutorial guides to effectively use the wiki pages. Alternatively, exploring external wiki editors might simplify the editing process. The academic team at Northumbria University is collaborating closely with IT systems and Learning Technology staff to determine what support is required to improve interactions and communications among the distributed teams in the Global Studio. This multidisciplinary research team is investigating technologies that would enable student groups to initiate teleconferences or videoconferences with counterparts at other universities. Data suggests that frequent videoconferencing between UK and USA student teams did not result in higher student satisfaction. These students reported the lowest satisfaction on most indicators in both progress and exit surveys. Another factor might have been that the industry partner in this project did not engage with the UK-based work teams until the mid-project progress review. From the lecturers' perspective, managing the three industry projects was complex. Consequently, to simplify communication and management, only one industry project was undertaken in the subsequent Global Studio. In conclusion, we suggest that Global Studio offers students a valuable learning environment. It exposes them to the complexities of communication and project management through design projects in distributed settings with international university and industry partners.
We wish to express our gratitude to our industry partners for their generous support, as well as to the participating academics and students. Special thanks go to Nick Oakley and Patrick Lynch from the Intel Mobility Group, Jerry Wright at Great Southern Wood Preserving, Inc., and Tsai Lu Liu from Auburn University. We also appreciate the contributions of Nicholas Jinkinson from the Motorola UK Design Centre and Ja-Sung Koo of Motorola/Consumer eXperience Design in Seoul, Korea. Additionally, we would like to recognize the assistance provided by Ben Lovatt from LTech, who was instrumental in supporting this project. Lastly, we are grateful for the research funding we received from CETL: AfL, ADM-HEA, and JISC infoNet.

INSTITUTIONALISING FUTURE GEOGRAPHIES OF FINANCIAL INCLUSION: NATIONAL LEGITIMACY VERSUS LOCAL AUTONOMY IN THE BRITISH CREDIT UNION MOVEMENT

PRE-PUBLICATION DRAFT SUBMITTED TO ANTIPODE 16/07/01  
Duncan Fuller, Division of Geography and Environmental Management, University of Northumbria at Newcastle, Newcastle upon Tyne, UK; e-mail: Duncan.Fuller@unn.ac.uk  
Andrew E G Jonas, Department of Geography, University of Hull, Hull, UK; e-mail: A.E.Jonas@geo.hull.ac.uk

In Great Britain, the challenges of financial withdrawal and the decline of community economies have highlighted the potential of local "alternative" financial setups to fight social and financial exclusion. This study explores one such entity, the residential or "community" credit union, which offers low-cost credit to members connected by a common bond area, often related to residence and/or workplace. Historically, community credit unions have been acknowledged for providing access to credit and savings in areas where mainstream financial services have been reduced. However, a shift from this traditional role is ongoing, posing three key challenges to the British credit union movement: (1) a dispute over redefining the "model" credit union nationwide; (2) evolving regulations for credit union growth, including aligning with New Labour's social exclusion initiatives; and (3) a "local" challenge involving credit unions in community economic development strategies. This paper discusses these challenges in the context of broader insights into the social dynamics, classification, and independence of local "alternative" financial institutions. The paper suggests that future research on financial inclusion geographies, especially regarding "alternative" systems and their ties to the financial mainstream, must critically examine contradictions and tensions across different spatial levels.

Introduction

Compared to the longstanding focus of economic geographers on production landscapes, research into financial institutions is relatively nascent (Martin 1999). This emerging field debates how to categorize the diverse institutions within the financial services "industry," often adopting terms like formal/informal, regulated/unregulated, high-street/network-based to describe similar institutions while casting differences in binary terms. For example, banks and building societies are often considered mainstream, formal, and economic-focused, contrasted with less visible, informal, or socially motivated entities (see Ford and Rowlingson 1994, 1996; Leyshon 1994; UK Social Investment Forum 1998). [Author's note: no reference for UK Social Investment Forum. Please complete.] More recently, attention has turned to the "alternative" nature of certain financial forms. This interest connects to the broader discourse on money's role in the space economy, emphasizing money as a "store of value" and a "social relation" (Martin 1999:11). [Author's note: Is this emphasis original?] This shift prompts research on social dynamics and geographical settings of local financial institutions and monies, including those believed to function semi-autonomously from mainstream sectors. It has been suggested that "local monies...offer diverse, possibly temporary, alternative ways of organizing local economies" (Lee 1999:223). The empowering potential of "alternative" financial systems is significant, especially against the backdrop of relentless global capital. This paper, however, interrogates the "alternative" label within British financial services' current landscape. Like the binaries discussed earlier, these forms are often seen as peripheral to a presumed non-alternative "core" of main banks and building societies. The paper argues that such binary categories may be misleading, as boundaries blur in a contemporary Britain exploring a "Third Way." [Author's note: Reconcile term's punctuation later in the text—"Third Way". Additionally, should this term be explained for readers?] Inspired by Roger Lee’s work on local monies (e.g., Lee 1996, 1999), we investigate community credit unions' ability to evolve into independent, sustainable alternatives to the financial mainstream. These are co-operative financial entities owned and managed by members from a common bond area, typically linked to residence or work. We are studying local capacities for credit union growth in select areas, integrating them into community economic development (CED) efforts, and examining larger trends within the credit union movement that affect local trajectories (Fuller and Jonas 1999a, b). This paper focuses on the linkage between local and national contexts in credit union development. It highlights how the British credit union role, identity, and philosophy are being redefined and granted legitimacy through state intervention in social exclusion policy. This shift has crucial implications for the future direction of credit unions in Britain, particularly in creating "spaces of hope" amid the "landscapes of poverty and despair" formed by uneven global finance dynamics. [Author's note: If the second quoted phrase is also by Harvey, please provide the page number; if not, it requires citation and pages.]

In Britain, credit unions have historically provided an accessible means of savings and loans for individual members (Fuller 1998b; McArthur, McGregor and Stewart 1993; National Consumer Council 1994). At a time when banks and building societies are downsizing and exiting many locales (Leyshon and Thrift 1997), credit unions—particularly community ones—potentially offer a more reliable financial presence for local residents, notably those with modest incomes. As Illsley and Jackson (1999:158) note, "Over the past two decades, as poverty increased and became spatially concentrated, residents from these areas have found affordable financial services increasingly inaccessible due to the modernization and rationalization of banks and building societies." This shouldn't imply that credit unions are the only financial alternative available or that replacing diminishing mainstream services is their sole impetus (Ford and Rowlingson 1996). Alongside other "local monies" like Local Exchange Trading Systems (LETS), credit unions are increasingly crucial for local financial stability and economic resilience amid restructuring and withdrawal (Conaty and Mayo 1997; Fitchew 1998). This status has gained additional prominence under the Labour Government, which now sees credit union support as vital to policy strategies addressing social and financial exclusion (Her Majesty’s Government 1999; Her Majesty’s Treasury 1998a, b, 1999a, b, c; Social Exclusion Unit 1998). Consistent with other "Third Way" politics under New Labour (Giddens 1998), the goal is not to disrupt global finance's dominance in the broader British economy but to bolster the development of alternative financial entities alongside mainstream economic frameworks. 

Acknowledging New Labour's increasing interest in defining credit unions, some movement representatives have advocated for redefining credit unions (Her Majesty’s Treasury 1999c:9). Here, we explore how this growing political validation may compromise credit unions' standalone role in particular areas. [Author's note: Are scare quotes necessary?] Evidently, a major attraction of community credit unions is their potential for providing genuine alternatives to mainstream financial services in localities. Accordingly, credit union growth has followed CED models informed by social capital and community empowerment concepts rather than traditional local economic growth theories, emphasizing "restructuring for community" over "restructuring for capital" (Haughton 1999a). [Author's note: Provide page numbers for quotes.] Traditionally, credit unions have been encouraged to develop separately from the financial mainstream, utilizing local associations, networks, and support often furnished by local authorities (see Illsley and Jackson 1999). However, we note that the predominant thrust in the credit union movement now trends toward forging increased connections with mainstream financial players and a commercially oriented national model rather than community-based initiatives. [Author's note: Are scare quotes needed?]

These competing models are shaping debates within the movement, influencing legislative reform discussions, and reflecting diverging views on credit unions' societal role. Thus, achieving locally autonomous development is likely to become increasingly challenging as the British credit union landscape continues to evolve. We organize our analysis around three primary challenges facing the credit union movement: first, the competing visions between advocates of the "old" community model and those on behalf of a "new" commercially oriented national model. [Author's note: Are scare quotes needed?] Second, we examine the efforts to influence credit union policy and regulation nationally, primarily through the Credit Union Taskforce's actions and progress on reforming what is often cited as "the most restrictive credit union law worldwide" (Fitchew 1998:1). Third, we address what we call the "local challenge" in credit union development: the idealized visions of community credit unions, the roles anticipated for them, and the often stark local development realities.

The concluding section discusses how these issues will concern both the movement itself and external parties in the forthcoming years.

Changes and Challenges I: Transforming the "Old" Credit Union Model

Within the British credit union framework, definitions of what a credit union represents and whom it serves have grown increasingly contentious. Historically, diverse philosophical and ideological views have been epitomized by major national credit union entities, namely the National Federation of Credit Unions (NFCU) and the Association of British Credit Unions Limited (ABCUL) (Berthoud and Hinton 1989). Although NFCU has recently undergone voluntary dissolution, some former members are forming a new organization with similar values. [Author's note: Should this sentence be moved to an endnote?]

These organizations actively participate in national discussions concerning the credit unions' future in Britain and their fight against social and financial exclusion. Traditionally, community credit unions have been perceived as "the poor person’s bank," a notion encouraged by numerous local authorities in Britain and promoted as a solution for "community" development. Community credit unions, specifically, have become central features in local anti-poverty agendas. While traditionally envisioned as mainly addressing financial necessities within impoverished communities, often described as "sink estates" (Barnekov and Jabber-Bey 1993; Illsley and Jackson 1999; McArthur, McGregor and Stewart 1993; contrast West 1999), their broader societal contribution has been seen as limited. Their actual impact in living up to such claims is probably even more limited (Fuller 1998b, 2000a). This belief is reinforced by research identifying some community credit unions’ apparent failure to generate the necessary income for fundamentally altering the financial situations of those residing within their designated common bond areas (Jones 1998b). It is now posited that many credit unions face challenges in becoming self-sustaining local credit sources precisely due to their efforts in fulfilling their community missions (Jones 1998b).

Simultaneously, there is widespread acknowledgment of tremendous growth potential within Britain's credit union landscape, alongside uncertainty regarding the shape this growth might take. Efforts are underway to shift the "old" model of credit union development to a "new," more comprehensive commercial model, potentially inspired by the U.S. approach, where credit unions function more like traditional banks (see Kaushik and Lopez 1994).

In Britain, credit unions have primarily emerged in old industrial zones and areas where the mainstream financial sector retreated. With over 600 credit unions registered nationwide, membership ranges from a mere 50 to a few thousand. Most are community-based, although the number of employer- and industrial-sector unions is on the rise. The movement maintains strong roots in Scotland, particularly urban centers like Strathclyde and Dundee (Illsley and Jackson 1999:158), Northern England (Manchester, Sheffield, and Newcastle), and the Midlands (Birmingham). The South of England is experiencing a surge in urban and rural credit unions. Growth potential is vast, especially as banks and building societies continue to shut branches. However, development models determine growth patterns in specific regions.

In pursuit of credit union expansion, emphasis is growing on the "health" and "success" of credit unions, notably community ones (see Jones 1998a). [Author's note: Are scare quotes needed for these two terms, here and below?] These factors are intertwined—perceptions of potential, success, and health intersect with critical questions about the movement’s future in the UK. Specifically tied to their contribution to exclusion policies, credit unions currently enjoy significant enthusiasm among UK policymakers and political figures (Fuller and Jonas 1999a, b, c). [Author's note: Fuller and Jonas 1999c missing reference. Please add.]

Credit union advocates urge capitalizing on this goodwill, leveraging positive perceptions to dismantle developmental barriers and establish genuine financial alternatives. Historically, "industrial" (employer-based) credit unions have been deemed easier to develop and manage than community-based ones. This results from the pre-existing membership fields, operational systems, and publicity channels existing within most employers that can be relatively inexpensively adapted for credit union functionality. In comparison, community credit unions rely on external organizational capacities such as volunteers or local authority-funded part-time staff (Illsley and Jackson 1999). Industrial credit unions are considered more "successful" based on asset/membership ratios. However, emerging evidence suggests this "success" relates more to the lack of community credit union advancement than specific industrial credit union achievements. [Author's note: Are italics necessary?] The point emphasized in Table 1, which details asset bases across union types, illustrates this. In 1996, residential credit unions outnumbered employer counterparts by over five to one yet demonstrated lower overall membership figures. Community credit unions reflected much lower average membership compared to employee-based unions. Many remain under 200 members, as was the case in June 1996, with eight of eleven Newcastle-upon-Tyne residential credit unions and four Dundee credit unions totaling just 1,500 members (Illsley and Jackson 1999). Importantly, residential credit unions comprised just 24.1% of overall union assets in 1996, despite representing over 45% of all members, a declining trend since the early '90s. Facing such developmental realities, questions arise about community credit unions' impact within common bond areas. Current credit union efforts aim to transform themselves into local, inclusive credit and finance providers. These efforts draw upon research from Liverpool John Moores University, ABCUL, English Community Enterprise Partnership, and the Co-operative Bank, with the Local Government Management Board and Local Government Association (Jones 1998a, b). [Author's note: Subsequent "Jones report" references refer to this study? Both Jones 1998a and 1998b or only one?] This research outlines several "issues" community credit unions encounter, including lack of growth, financial self-sufficiency, and volunteer reliance (Jones 1998b:4). [Author's note: Are scare quotes needed?]

Continuing, the study indicates the "old" model's ultimate unsustainability, favoring community engagement and volunteer capacity-building over delivering quality financial services to all qualifying common bond members. [Author's note: Clarify "qualifying" here.] During a recent Local Economy Policy Unit seminar, a senior ABCUL figure referred to the model as "flawed." Given limited expansion potential under the "old" model, credit unions are advised to shift toward a "new" one. The Jones report (1998b) suggests redefining "small," reorienting volunteer roles, adopting professionalism in service provision, and hiring paid staff for daily operations. These adaptations might prompt mergers, acquisitions, or closures among community credit unions. If changes aren't pursued, "old" model groups would struggle, failing to contribute to broader societal aims without greater support. For example, a community development worker in Kingston-upon-Hull—focusing on impoverished peripheral housing estates—contended it would take considerable time to reach the most in need, if ever. [Author's note: Source of this argument?] Such unions would persist, highly dependent on volunteer aid and state support for survival. Hence, making Britain's credit unions financially and socially sustainable seemingly requires rebranding the "old" model into a commercially viable, mutually supportive, and inclusive "new" model. However, consensus on this trajectory remains elusive within the credit union movement. For instance, NACUW voices reservations regarding certain reported aspects (NACUW 1999b). While aligning with concerns about failing unions, NACUW (1999b:2) cautions against sacrificing economic goals for simply becoming another financial institution. The report critiques characterizing community unions as "voluntary sector" businesses, advocating instead for "community-based, or owned, mutual financial institutions." NACUW argues for greater emphasis on national entities’ roles, like ABCUL and the Registry of Friendly Societies, in the persistent small-scale volunteer operations in community credit unions.

Signs of a potential rift in the movement are visible regarding credit unions' future growth. The transformative "old" model agenda aligns more closely with instrumentalist credit union development views (Berthoud and Hinton 1989). Unsurprisingly, ABCUL's philosophical leanings support these moves, leveraging recent research to further its objectives, notably within Her Majesty’s Treasury 1999a, b, c and Local Government Association 1999 reports. [Author's note: Specify claims or moves. Local Government Association reference missing; please add.]

Analyzing how credit union ideations are received within audiences is crucial, as the "new" model reimagines what success and alternatives mean for credit unions (Fuller and Jonas 1999a, b, c). Furthermore, attention should be paid to interactions between members, local unions, and national bodies to understand transformations at the grassroots level. In this light, credit unions' role amid wider social exclusion and financial reform debates in Britain emerges as a key area for scrutiny.

Changes and Challenges II: New Labour Policies on Social Exclusion and Financial Reform in the UK

Recent scholarly interest in "local monies" has sparked investigations into institutions not directly linked to mainstream financial channels. Our initial focus on community credit unions stemmed from their assumed "alternative" credit sources. Ironically, credit unions’ continued evolution in Britain might require stronger ties with mainstream entities. This connects to how national credit union movements seek to influence regulatory frameworks perceived as empowering financially and socially (Fuller and Jonas 1999a, b). Yet, it seems parts of the movement, especially ABCUL, are influencing these debates more effectively.

The second challenge the movement faces involves rapidly changing policy and regulatory contexts affecting credit union growth and impacted by specific ideological viewpoints. Credit unions are increasingly absorbed into mainstream policymaking in Britain. Under Prime Minister Tony Blair, New Labour has underscored credit unions’ roles in combatting social exclusion and finance withdrawal (Fitchew 1998; Social Exclusion Unit 1998). Documents from Her Majesty’s Government, crafted by entities like the Credit Union Taskforce and PAT 14, depict credit unions favorably but with ambiguities around their precise policy role. Credit union development meshes with elements of Third Way politics, where New Labour maintains global finance's British economic leadership while fostering entities like credit unions to tackle withdrawal and exclusion issues. At the same time, initiatives develop to integrate "alternative" entities like credit unions with the financial mainstream. Established in 1998, the Credit Union Taskforce aims to help low-income individuals access financial services, exploring collaborations between credit unions, banks, and building societies. Overseen by Royal Bank of Scotland’s Deputy Group Chief Executive Fred Goodwin, the taskforce comprises senior bank, building society, and movement representatives (Her Majesty’s Treasury 1998c). Its mission includes identifying best practices and proposing new collaborations for effective credit unions, expanding services, and aiding movement growth (Her Majesty’s Treasury 1998b). Similarly, PAT 14, one of 18 teams tackling exclusion, emphasizes broadening financial service access (Social Exclusion Unit 1998). Both reflect New Labour's commitment to assigning more prominent roles to credit unions in addressing exclusion. The government seeks to enhance service access, with recommendations extending to credit unions and the broader financial services sector. Helen Liddell, then Economic Secretary to the Treasury, stated, "Credit unions can offer low-income savings and credit solutions. They also provide a 'financial ladder's first rung for young people. We want to harness that potential. Collaborative bank-credit union efforts could offer access to accounts and credit for more people" (Her Majesty’s Treasury 1998c:1). There is also growing recognition of obstacles to British credit union development along lines noted by the Jones report.

Subsequent initiatives emphasize "boosting" credit union growth, focusing on regulatory changes and a new Central Services Organization designed to support roles (Her Majesty’s Treasury 1999a:1). [Author's note: Are scare quotes necessary?]

Regulatory Changes for Credit Unions

Regulations governing credit union activity date back to the 1979 Act. Recent Treasury-initiated proposals highlight changes that will influence credit union operations. These efforts seek to "promote growth while ensuring credit unions focus on serving society's less affluent members" (Her Majesty’s Treasury 1998b:1). Financial reform signifies an initial step towards a new regulatory framework impacting this "alternative" sector and its mainstream ties. While 1996’s financial deregulation didn't satisfy dissatisfaction with existing legislation, new reforms address criticism of the 1979 Act and justify financial reform necessity with three key points:

1. The 1979 Act severely limits the range of member services and funding options for credit unions.  
2. The established supervision and regulation methods are rudimentary and constrain the Registry’s intervention powers. Options are limited to inaction or closure.  
3. UK credit unions lack a share protection scheme, and enacting statutory requirements is the fastest, surest means to establish one. (Fitchew 1998:1–2)

Deregulatory measures aim to improve legislative conditions, building on 1997 Inter-Association Legislative Liaison Group (IALLG) suggestions. Participants from ABCUL, NACUW, NFCU, AICU, and SLCU contributed to the report "Common Ground: National Goals for Improving Credit Union Laws," arguing current laws hinder movement growth and member needs service (IALLG 1997:1). These principles guided the 1998 Treasury consultation document, initial reform proposals, and final recommendations, including longer loan terms, lenient common bond rules, and changes in maximum account holdings, among others (Her Majesty’s Treasury 1999b). The aim is to alleviate 1979 Act restrictions collectively, though this also implies all credit unions should follow and benefit from these changes, irrespective of identity, priorities, or outlooks.

Accompanying these measures, and given the skepticism surrounding the current system’s efficacy (Her Majesty’s Treasury 1999c:11), a new regulatory framework is proposed via the Financial Services Authority (FSA). Both PAT 14 and the Credit Union Taskforce’s reports advocate for effective regulation to protect depositors, build trust, and ensure service quality. There's acknowledgement of a gradual reform process’s necessity because abrupt changes might threaten community credit unions’ survival, as foreseen in the Jones report.

Two key issues linger in financial reform discussions. First are FSA fees for credit unions compared to other financial entities, with implications for small credit union viability. Second is allowing "proportionality," a concept requiring room for smaller unions' growth, provided they seem viable, versus exterminating them (Social Exclusion Unit 1999:17). The PAT 14 report underscores these potential benefits and indicates the need for readiness among credit unions to capitalize on emerging opportunities, contingent on targeted encouragement (Social Exclusion Unit 1999:13).

Central Services Organization (CSO)

CSO concepts emerge from contexts where credit unions thrive with supportive CSOs (Her Majesty’s Treasury 1999c). [Author's note: Are scare quotes needed?] International examples show several potential CSO services like back-office processing, business planning aid, financial education, marketing, treasury management, and more (Her Majesty’s Treasury 1999c:13; Social Exclusion Unit 1999:16). However, how these align with community-focused agendas is unclear.

CSO’s structure—single UK body or federal/regional model—is undecided. It may encompass local authority roles, channeling funds for credit union service provision, potentially standardizing "local" approaches consistent with central and ABCUL views. [Author's note: Previous benefit of such consistency?] In addition, CSOs would likely partner with local agencies in organizational and development roles, though influence distribution is unknown. The hope is a unified organization bridging movement philosophical divides, as PAT 14 report states that CSO establishment would centralize movement focus (Social Exclusion Unit 1999:19). However, this could also negate differences, pushing towards prescribed development paths for benefitting from available services. [Author's note: Are scare quotes on "beneifts" needed, here and next?]

Potential "rewards" for embracing this include possible bank and building society support, such as capital for CSO establishment, material donations like premises or equipment, and staff secondments. While still under consultation, these proposals reveal a developing relationship between ABCUL and the government rooted in specific premises from the Jones Report. With state appropriation under selective instrumentalist guise, issues of defining credit unions relative to mainstream financial players must be addressed.

There's a possibility of credit unions being shaped into second-tier banking services, allowing main players to focus on wealthier clients and offload residual moral duty on another "alternative" sector, yet one different in scope and sense from recently studied academic examples. As a significant phase in British credit union development—and idealist credit union futures suggested (Berthoud and Hinton 1989)—we must consider political implications and beneficiary clarity. An inquiry should assess original goals aligning with highlighted developmental shifts, pondering if Britain’s credit unions will serve as genuine alternatives or simply appendages to the mainstream. Overall, further research might explore these institutions’ alternative futures compared to local monetary systems, examining their fit within Blair's exclusion narrative. [Author's Note: Suggest alternate for double "alternative" or retain both?]

On a "local" level in relation to CED initiatives, the synergy of "national" strategies, credit union bodies, existing approaches, and governance will require evaluation. [Author's note: Are scare quotes necessary?] Briefly examined here as the third challenge, we acknowledge institutional development in years ahead.

Changes and Challenges III: The "Local" Challenge

The third facet of the credit union movement addresses local experiences’ potential influences on the broader movement’s trajectory. With movement shifts and regulatory and organizational changes looming, national strategies will impact—possibly redirect—local developments. Simultaneously, development pathways already visible at the local level mirror and contribute to ongoing national debates. Historically reliant on community organizational capacities since its inception (in Britain, the 1960s), this paradigm is now shifting: national and local influence on trajectories grows increasingly interconnected. Previously, aside from workers and volunteers, pivotal development figures were local authorities granting feasibility research, premises, and sometimes staffing. Now, the changing nature of local authority-credit union support varies by region, particularly depending on whether development is identified locally as "community development," "community economic development," or "local economic development" (see Fuller 1997). [Author's note: Need quotes on "support"? If quoted phrases are source, provide pages.]

Furthermore, the relationship is evolving not only due to local governance shifts in Britain (see Cochrane 1993, e.g.) but also because credit unions reconsider, analyze, or implement the generalized development models such as those from the Jones report. One key area for potential local change is the increasing legitimacy of CED initiatives. These have thrived across Britain and Europe amid manufacturing-dependent regions’ deindustrialization and national and EU community regeneration funding (see Amin, Cameron and Hudson 1998, 1999; Mayer 1998; Regional Studies Association 1997, e.g.). While community credit unions are now studied for their role in CED and regeneration (West 1999), a holistic understanding of effective short- or long-term development strategies based on specific economic and political conditions remains elusive. This knowledge gap is significant considering attempts to "standardize" strategies through entities like the CSO. [Author's Note: Are scare quotes needed?]

CED initiatives in Britain target labor market flexibility, unemployment, and social exclusion (see Haughton 1999b; Lawless et al 1998; Regional Studies Association 1997, e.g.). Haughton (1999a) describes CED as emphasizing strategies encouraging "restructuring for community" instead of "restructuring for capital" (Haughton 1999a). [Author's note: Quote page numbers needed.] These strategies focus on creating socially beneficial goods, addressing local needs in ways maximizing benefits for residents (Haughton 1999a:15). Grounded in networks and partnerships not necessarily linked to conventional local economic development, they are promoted by actors operating separately from dominant governance (Clavel 1986; Fitzgerald 1991; Haughton and While 1999; Jonas 1995). Filion (1998:1115) asserts that CED often features a local culture determined to survive economically adverse conditions. Credit unions fit within this view of CED. Yet like Haughton’s (1999a:16) suggestion that there isn’t one CED "model," distinguishing between community-centric and mainstream local development strategies could grow more complex practically. In Britain, determining which credit union "model" suits local contexts and how national progress affects local strategies will be pivotal. The "new" model from the Jones report might not align with community-based development. While strategic options still exist locally in terms of appropriate and sustainable credit union growth, potential conflict and suppressing diversity could arise.

Community credit unions must decide on nurturing closer mainstream financial relationships while exploring local and broader funding opportunities. This may mean engaging strategies beyond those solely highlighting credit union growth as CED aspects. Even within CED, as national policies gain traction, credit union organizers should interact with larger institutional scales beyond local areas (like local authorities) to secure resources and financial aid. Consequently, development strategies within and beyond localities will determine community credit union trajectories. As local and national dimensions influence British financial "alternatives," they are increasingly intertwined. [Author's Note: Repeated from opening phrase of the above paragraph, beginning "This is now changing..."]

Interestingly, amid discussions about credit unions’ organizational "right way," CED research shifts from general "best practice" understanding to specific initiative-contextual analysis. [Author's Note: Scare quotes on "best practice" needed?] Studies have exposed CED’s varied forms across localities and how experiences could shape broader exclusion-combatting policies (Amin, Cameron and Hudson 1998, 1999; Haughton 1999b; Mayer 1998). Thus, one local challenge may involve community credit unions' increased CED focus or incorporation. Diverse local approaches may produce divergent development strategies, goals, and consequences, offering insights into their social contributions. Defining a "successful" credit union may differ across areas, prompting movement organizers to reflect on varied local progress, collaborative partnerships, supportive mechanisms, and governance—and how these paths affect broader spatial scales. [Author's Note: Suggest synonyms for “wide range” double occurrence or retain both?]

Conclusions

This paper presents preliminary thoughts on community credit unions' potential roles in forming financially sustainable, socially inclusive British communities. Key challenges and changes the movement will encounter are identified. Notably, the sometimes conflicting drive towards financial stability versus social inclusiveness aligns with debates about which development "model" to pursue. The "old" model provided community access to finance amid mainstream sector withdrawal but its limits are now under scrutiny, with calls for commercialization and mainstream financial ties through a "new" model. Meanwhile, national regulatory and political changes are poised to impact credit union growth paths regionally. Local challenges persist, specifically in leveraging strategic community capacities fostered by CED initiatives. The British credit union movement risks developing a "two-tiered" structure relegating community unions to "second-class" status, tackling problems induced by mainstream entities. [Author's note: Are scare quotes necessary?] Smaller, idealist credit unions may become marginalized further by the evolving hierarchy. Although not inevitable, each consultation cycle supports this trend. Consequently, movement activists must confront challenging development model decisions. Continuing community-oriented growth may cause practical funding and political support challenges, necessitating re-evaluation in light of alternative support or scales, e.g., from central or EU sources. Conversely, defending "old" models could suppress potential growth or broader agendas. Thus, locally identifying sustainable credit union models and redefining "success" in both local and national contexts is paramount. Credit unions may blend into various developmental forms—community, economic, or mainstream—depending on perspectives. As the community’s precise and role diminishes in credit union evolution, further analysis of their local manifestations' implications is needed.

This survey of future challenges suggests research directions concerning geographies of "local monies" and alternative financial forms’ social relations. One anticipated focus is alternative financial bodies’ independence from economic mainstreams. The "local monies" concept hinges on autonomy from financial mainstreams, preserving local character. However, British credit unions, amid regulatory and banking sector involvement changes, render this increasingly questionable. Linkage enhancement, partially through achieving commercial "success", may risk losing community identity and autonomy. Still, questioning if "local monies" requires mainstream disengagement and local capacity dependency in development remains pertinent. Avoiding assumptions that community unions will progress unfettered without considering broader contexts is crucial. The core concern is not whether credit unions retain some institutional "autonomy," but engagement with external environments and subsequent sustainability and inclusiveness.

Spatial scale emerges crucially as financial services sector boundaries redefine domestically. Lessons may still be gleaned from Harvey's exploration of US housing finance (Harvey 1974, 1985). He distinguished "parochial" efforts—splintering neighborhoods against each other without average material condition change—from "nonparochial" movements—mobilizing wider scale organizational capacities against exclusion. [Author's Note: In which cited Harvey publication do these concepts appear? Are scare quotes needed?]

For British credit unions, relating community development within a scalar politics—working through movement internal politics and national financial reregulation—is advantageous. Yet empowering individuals isn’t just about scaling activities. "Empowerment" involves multiple scales, up and down, simultaneously (Jonas 1994:261). Hence, British financial "autonomy" as a scalar-strategic issue hinges on whether credit union stakeholders can and want community credit unions to remain mainstream detached. This depends on locality development strategies’ nature, philosophies underpinning these strategies—at least partly shaped by broader movement influences—and their engagements with local, national, or international resources and policy contexts. Encouraging credit union growth through stronger regulation and assistance holds potential for more inclusive institutions, locally and nationally. Yet, linking credit unions to the mainstream risks perpetuating existing uneven financial withdrawal patterns. Strategic focus might emphasize community development within financially excluded areas, but awareness of community creditors’ universal strategies' global implications is imperative. Filion (1998) suggests community-based frameworks remain vital to alternative post-Fordism paths. The credit union movement aligns central to Britain's "alternative" pathway definition battles.
