"Tractatus Linguistico-Therapeuticus"— Towards a Theory of Therapeutic Language  
Patrick Jemmer  

This and future articles draw upon Wittgenstein's idea of a "philosophical therapy for (and through) language" and a "linguistic therapy for (and through) philosophy.” The focus is on the critical link between the "private" or "internal" language use, which is thought to mediate self-awareness, and how people "operate" in the "real" world using "public" language. Although we may effortlessly engage in linguistic interaction, it becomes clear that philosophical dilemmas tied to the nature and process of such "intrapersonal communication" are intrinsically complex. The arguments concerning the potential and significance of a fundamentally "Private Language" are explored, as are the implications of these arguments when applying communication theory to self-awareness. It is emphasized that it is essential for the professional communicator, especially the therapist, to understand these issues, which underpin contemporary linguistic therapy and therapeutic linguistics. To comprehend Wittgenstein’s concept of "the misuse of language as the origin of philosophical befuddlement," we retrace our steps to consider the "Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus," the work defining Wittgenstein’s initial approach to philosophy with language at its center. The opening line is striking: ‘The world is everything that is the case’ [0]. Even though we might think "there is no identifiable overriding theory," Wittgenstein clarifies in the Preface of the Tractatus that "The book deals with philosophical problems and shows, I believe, that the method of formulating these problems rests on misunderstanding the logic of our language. Its meaning can be summed up this way: What can be said at all can be said clearly; and whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent" [1]. Thus, as we unravel the "tangled threads" of Wittgenstein’s philosophical thinking, we enter a "surrogationalist" world of "mystical solipsism," where "philosophy is not a silent practice" [2], and where the key principles are: "(i) words have meanings by ‘standing for’ entities, properties, relations, etc., and (ii) these entities, properties, relations, etc., exist independently of the words representing them" [3]. Therefore, "In the Tractatus world, symbols can either say something about the world (describing) or show something about the world (revealing ontological structure)" [4]. For example, "Propositions like ‘It is raining’ convey something true or false; contradictions and tautologies, on the other hand, are neither – they show the world’s structure, indicating that combining certain signs creates contradictions or tautologies" [4]. Wittgenstein takes us from the world to the heart of problems and solutions, i.e., the proposition, through the concept of a thought. After urging us to view the world as composed of facts, not things, Wittgenstein introduces the central idea of picturing the world's facts [5]. Wittgenstein elaborates that "We picture facts... A picture models reality... Objects within a picture correspond to picture elements... These elements represent objects... The specific arrangement of these elements constitutes a picture... A picture is a fact... Every picture inherently shares logical form with reality to depict it, correctly or incorrectly... A logical picture models facts as a thought... In a proposition, thought is perceptibly expressed through the senses" [1]. If "the world is everything that is the case," then "... A thought is a proposition with meaning... The totality of propositions is language... A proposition models reality as we imagine it" [1]. The nature of these "pictures" requires reflection since "At first glance, a proposition, like one printed, doesn’t seem to picture the reality in question. Written notes don't seem initially to picture a piece of music, nor do phonetic notations picture speech. Yet, these sign-languages are pictures of what they represent" [1]. This shows how important it is in Wittgenstein’s analysis that facts are articulate, making them picturable, corresponding picture elements to objects constituting the fact [5]. Thus, we grasp Wittgenstein’s aphorism: "The limits of my language are the limits of my world" [1], and he intends the Tractatus to "draw a boundary to thinking, or rather – to the expression of thoughts; to draw a boundary, we must think both sides of it (thus think what cannot be thought). The boundary can thus be drawn only in language, and what lies beyond must simply be nonsense" [1]. In conclusion, the core idea of the Tractatus suggests "all philosophical propositions are nonsensical, including those in Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus, echoing the Tao Tê Ching: ‘The Tao that can be expressed is not the eternal Tao’” [5]. Monk summarizes that "The Tractatus’s main point answers the ‘central problem of philosophy,’ i.e., establishing the limits of expressibility" [5]. Importantly, "In providing what he saw as a definitive answer, Wittgenstein thought he resolved all philosophical issues, specifically defining ethics. In logic and ethics, the same central point is essential: ‘Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent’” [5]. Thus, on one hand, "By holding that only elementary, logically independent, fact-stating propositions have meaning, the Tractatus dooms itself to transgress these limits. Its propositions are elucidations and tautologies, saying nothing, and like all philosophical utterances, are nonsensical efforts to say the unsayable" [2], yet, on the other, it "successfully conveys an unassailable philosophical truth: all philosophical speech results in nonsense, shown as its propositions are nonsense because they try to say something philosophical" [5]. We will later examine these arguments' validity related to the human psyche, self-awareness, intrapersonal communication, and mysticophilosophicolinguistic therapy via a journey in Eden – “That spot to which I point is Paradise, / Adams abode, those lofty shades his Bowre” [6] – where our mythical ancestors’ “Unspeakable desire to see and know,” and choice to “speak rather than remain silent,” their “profoundly nonsensical efforts to say the unsayable,” result in new awareness and life forms, and a new language game. So, we turn to “midnight in the garden of good and evil” [7], to Adam and Eve, and question whether, by "transgressing the limits" and eating "the fruit of that forbidden tree," [6], Adam Namer confusedly muttered meanings to his mate, or Chava solipsistically spoke to herself, realizing “What thou seest, / What there thou seest fair Creature is thy self, / With thee it came and goes…” [6] in their blooming self-awareness? Thus, that insightful eve, "Damn!" Adam might declare to Eve: "Madam in Eden I’m Adam!" – as both " ... aware themselves, and soon / In order, quit of all impediment" [6] – and with correct phrasing, we witness recursion at work, a step from the primordial adventure described in previous articles [8] – [14]. First, "The human animal alone talks to itself. It sustains a continual inner dialogue, approving or disapproving its actions, or itself. Its self-accusations and defences differ in external dialogues. The self pities and glorifies, accuses and excuses. It couldn’t dialogue without its ‘reason’; as the dialogue makes the self in one role the object of thought. It uses conceptual images" [15]. This awareness is crucial because in Edenic terms, "The mind is its own place, and can make a Heav’n of Hell, a Hell of Heav’n" [6], as Hamlet knew, explaining Yahweh’s fruit prohibition. Below, we'll explore self-awareness believed to depend on secretive language [15]. "Self-talk is ongoing dialogue determining behavior" [16] and after joining Adam and Eve, we'll see that "Internal dialogue's concept, specifically positive and negative thoughts' polarity, has historical roots from Plato to William James" [17]. These foundational polarities have significant consequences; "Initially distinguishing world from self leads, through language, to self–world distinction. World separation only incites world and self consciousness as world objects. Self-awareness needs further self-differentiation – language meets this need" [18]. Concerning self and surrounding awareness, and self-in-surroundings, we recognize that "Our reliance on language for communication requires assigning word-labels to surrounding phenomena. We refer to phenomena by labels, as if the label is the phenomenon, instead of shorthand. It's easier to say 'That’s a cow,' than 'That is something to which our culture, by general agreement, assigns the label ‘cow’. In science, too, it's convenient to talk of atomic structure like atoms have protons, neutrons, electrons, though modern physics differs" [19]. Thus, "Confusion arises when thinking of labels as the phenomena they represent... Everything except the phenomenon is abstract; naming erodes experiential immediacy, raising a wall between phenomenon and self when a construct or definition is given" [19]. Essentially, "Beyond the world and outside language lies meaning's source... This 'outside' encompasses sacred, ethical, and aesthetic value. Genuine propositions can't exist about these values because they show themselves in saying, and what can be shown can't be said" [2]. We might ask if Adam was "stuck wanting more than his thoughts for company" [20], realizing that "… we can't talk about much that fascinates us – natural theology, metaphysical cosmology, ethics, and aesthetics – without falling into nonsense" [2], thus contemplating thought? "Towards the end of Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus, Wittgenstein states: ‘There is indeed the inexpressible. It is the mystical.' Among things 'showing themselves' are ethics, aesthetics, religion, life's meaning, logic, and philosophy. Wittgenstein suggests truths exist in these areas but can't be expressed in language; they must be shown, not said" [5]. Belief in the "inexpressible, mystical" where "omen nomen nemoni hominis [est]" – “An omen to none is the name of a man” – raises the question whether “... a word, a name (nomen), can conjure destiny (omen), determining the future” [21]. The issue's core is "This is where language fails. All language is abstract. Language limits require abstraction, as conveying full experience through words is impossible. Descriptions beyond ‘is-ness’ are culturally determined and limit perception to cultural parameters. Communication imperatives force language to gain agreement on consensual reality, and experiential reality suffers as language embeds in cultural mindset" [19]. Furthermore, humans insist on inventing concepts beyond "consensual reality," and "Wittgenstein held moral and sacred values as inexpressible... Always thinking philosophizing wasn't theorizing; no business in scientific explanation... Philosophy was elucidatory, resulting in proposition clarification" [2]. Following this, "Wittgenstein emphasized philosophical problems arise from people's conditions, focusing on them rather than impersonal concrete or abstract features" [22]. "Philosophy can’t show what science’s propositions say. It gives no explanations, and makes no scientific discoveries; thus, mistakes can't happen in philosophy. Philosophy also can't say what aesthetic, moral, and sacred values show in language, despite the tendency" [2]. We might guess that in his "education towards independence" [23], and drawn by "no mistakes in philosophy," Wittgenstein "succumbed to language's inherent temptation to 'grasp essence,’... proposing an internal logical structure for language to anchor it to the world" [2]. Regarding the Tractatus, "The outcome is a curious hybrid, a logic treatise and a mystical viewpoint expression... Russell was shocked at his 'dream' student's transformation from war experiences. 'I sensed a mystical flavor in his book,' he wrote to Ottoline Morrell…" [5]. This "mystical philosophy" or "philosophical mysticism," concerning self-awareness and therapeutic change, underpins this article. At this point, we revisit Hegel's idea that "to be conscious of the world, I must be aware of being conscious" and examine how information from the external world is filtered (internally, mentally, emotionally, verbally, perceptually) before forming internal representations [24]. This filtering mediates our meta-meaning-making process, crafting our self-image. We respond to these filtered perceptions, not a true external "reality." We must constantly verify perceptions and test assumptions instead of treating them as facts. Moreover, adopting Kant's stance: "We comprehend the universe only as filtered through subjectivity's constitutive categories" [23], the "split between the knowledge Subject (knower) and the knowledge Object (known) replicates in the Subject itself" [23]. We frame this with communication theory by stating that individuals "exist in a dynamic relation with each other and contexts. Contexts interrelation (including living conditions), metaprogrammes, [instructions, control of programs] and expectations leads to activities fulfilling perceived needs. Activities change metaprogrammes, affect contexts and create new expectations. This represents an ongoing dynamic process, not a linear chain" [25], [26]. Chomsky was asked about human reality creation: "How does language affect consciousness and reality?" [27] He replied, "[It's] mostly by introspection, If you pay attention, you find constant self-talk. It’s hard to experience moments without internal dialogue – it's a major part of consciousness, and it uses language. Language affects thought and awareness, but specifics are tricky. We only access thought or consciousness through language, complicating the question" [27]. Language and experience link because "We learn language by internalizing verbal labels as sensory input shorthand; when recalling a sensory matrix, we subvocalize its label. Internal dialogue is assumed persistent during sensory labeling by subvocalization, with culture-approved nouns, verbs, and adjectives. This mandatory internal dialogue limits potential since labels are treated as things" [19] – as seen earlier. "This language-limited human potential is visible in children’s faces. Pre-verbal kids glow in awe, newly exposed to language swim in potential... Eventually, schooling and pressure for continuous inner dialogue lead to facial closure... During late adolescence or early adulthood, the face shows conviction that little is possible" [19]. Anecdotal firsthand evidence suggests "brain injuries can interrupt inner speech. Like an imaginary drug. Scott Moss, a psychologist, experienced a strokes, losing language capability but recuperated and shared his experience" [28] saying "I lost the ability to converse... and engage in self-talk. I couldn't think about the future – worry, anticipate, perceive – at least not verbally. For weeks post-hospitalization I simply existed." Morin [28] concludes, "Inner speech awareness emerges from mental processes interpretation. Moss couldn’t self-discuss mind events, so he just existed. He had feelings, perceptions, but awareness was vague – if present; foresight was impossible." The large-scale philosophical essence was recognized by Hegel. "His philosophy holds memory of humanity piecing fragmented remnants, seeking historical self-realization's significance. Humanity claims its past whole, self-awareness transforming to self-consciousness – or realizing existing consciousness is already self-aware" [23]. We delve into "self-awareness" where "‘self-awareness’ needs careful definition... it refers to the ability to become one's focus [29], actively identifying, processing, and storing self-information. It involves recognizing one's mental states (perceptions, sensations, attitudes, intentions, emotions, etc.) and public self-characteristics (behaviors and physical appearance)" [30]. Hegel asserted, "To be conscious, I must also be conscious of being conscious. Self-consciousness is integral to consciousness. The two-way (subject/object) relation becomes complex with awareness of others' presence. Self-consciousness (in-itself) lacks real subjectivity" [23]. "Self-consciousness (subjectivity) initially perceives lack – the object. Freedom originates here, with Desire. It is aware of its unity and purpose. But, it's also divided, isolated from other consciousnesses. For humanity to self-consciously guide its history, Hegel must relate individual self-consciousnesses essentially. He must reconcile freedom's divide-and-unite effect on humans" [23]. Today, self-awareness mainly derives from social (reflected appraisal, perspectives, audiences), physical environments (mirrors, cameras, photos, media), and the self (inner speech, imagery, dual stimulation) [30]. These may "divide, and ultimately unite, human individuals." The critical link between human operation contexts, "metaprogrammes" controlling actions, and future expectations is said to be mediated through language, "Wittgenstein holds all world knowledge, all thought, talk, and such, roots in experience, interaction, action, i.e., linguistic environmental processes" [26]. The problem with this restriction on our knowledge is that “In this way, our everyday language masks thoughts’ logical forms. Philosophy, Wittgenstein believes, involves confusion-induced problems due to this disguise. Re-expressing thoughts in Frege and Russell’s formal languages often helps" [5]. A key consequence of "all knowledge is gained linguistically" is "One can't exist as a social being outside a social framework; this framework is mediated by shared language. In the long run, no private language exists with communicative function. Understanding oneself (identity) is revealed through interaction. 'No one is an island'" [26]. This ties into Wittgenstein’s Private Language Argument and its mystico-philosophical debate about "private language" having any communicative function or its usefulness, explored later in detail. Consequently, the impact of our language on external and reflexively internal worlds is that "one doesn’t enter an environment without effecting it. Effects are interactions, or lead to or avoid interaction, itself interaction. Achieving ‘objectivity’ in environments is impossible. Not recognizing language’s illusory aspects leads to poor outcomes... Gaining system information requires entering, altering its conditions, discussing it" [26]. Thus, languaging applies a kind of ironic magic on our reflexive self-existence because "There is no subjectivity or objectivity. Observers’ presence, inside or outside, changes processes within the observed environment" [26]. The result is that "If our reality constructs arise from internal dialogue interpreting sensory input, then each dialogue's uniqueness means no common mutual reality exists" [19]. The nature and outcomes of this uncertain, self-languaging process in creating, maintaining, and changing human realities are extensively examined in the next article.
